{{Short description|Parliamentary constituency in the United Kingdom, 1885–1950 and 2024 onwards}} {{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}} {{Infobox UK constituency |name = Spen Valley |type = County |parliament = uk |image = {{maplink|frame=yes|frame-align=center|plain=yes|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/Spen Valley (UK Parliament constituency)}}|frame-height=200|frame-width=250}} |caption = Boundaries since 2024 |image2 = [[File:Yorkshire and the Humber - Spen Valley constituency.svg|215px|alt=Map of constituency]] |caption2 = Boundary of Spen Valley in Yorkshire and the Humber |year = 2024 |abolished = |elects_howmany = One |previous = {{ubl|[[Batley and Spen (UK Parliament constituency)|Batley and Spen]]|[[Dewsbury (UK Parliament constituency)|Dewsbury]] (part)|[[Huddersfield (UK Parliament constituency)|Huddersfield]] (minor part)}} |next = |year2 = 1885 |abolished2 = 1950 |elects_howmany2 = One |previous2 = [[Eastern West Riding of Yorkshire (UK Parliament constituency)|Eastern West Riding of Yorkshire]] |next2 = [[Batley and Morley]], [[Brighouse and Spenborough]] and [[Dewsbury (UK Parliament constituency)|Dewsbury]] |region = England |county = [[West Yorkshire]] |towns = {{ubl|[[Mirfield]]|[[Birstall, West Yorkshire|Birstall]]|[[Gomersal]]|[[Heckmondwike]]|[[Cleckheaton]]}} |mp = [[To be confirmed|TBC]] |party = }} '''Spen Valley''' is a [[United Kingdom constituencies|parliamentary constituency]] in the valley of the [[River Spen]] in the [[West Riding of Yorkshire]]. It returned one [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Member of Parliament]] (MP) to the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom]].
Further to the completion of the [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], the seat will be re-established for the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]], formed primarily from the (to be abolished) constituency of [[Batley and Spen]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Yorkshire and the Humber {{!}} Boundary Commission for England |url=https://boundarycommissionforengland.independent.gov.uk/2023-review/yorkshire-and-the-humber/ |access-date=2023-06-15 |website=boundarycommissionforengland.independent.gov.uk}}</ref>
==History==
The constituency was created by the [[Redistribution of Seats Act 1885]] for the [[1885 United Kingdom general election|1885 general election]], retained with altered boundaries in 1918, and abolished for the [[1950 United Kingdom general election|1950 general election]]. In the 1901 Census, there were 13,557 inhabited houses in the division; there were 10,960 registered electors, of which 9,396 qualified by virtue of occupying property within the division, 1,490 by virtue of owning property, 67 by virtue of occupying land only within the division, and 7 qualifying as lodgers.<ref>"Parliamentary Constituencies (Electors, &c.) (United Kingdom)", House of Commons Paper no. 85 of session 1901, p. 7.</ref>
Political historian [[Henry Pelling]] noted that the constituency as it existed from 1885 to 1918 was dominated by the woollen industry and carpetmaking, where the vast bulk of the population were [[Nonconformist (Protestantism)|nonconformist]]: the Church of England parish of Birstall was said to have had only four clergymen in the eighteenth century (two of whom were schoolmasters).<ref>[[Henry Pelling]], "Social Geography of British Elections 1885-1910", Macmillan, 1967, p. 302.</ref> In 1922, membership of nonconformist circuits in the constituency is estimated at 2,759 for the [[Congregational Church]], 1,065 [[Wesleyanism]], 1,027 [[United Methodist Church]], 698 [[Primitive Methodism]], and 328 [[Baptists]], making it the second largest nonconformist attendance in the West Riding.<ref>Michael Kinnear, "The British Voter" 2nd edition, Batsford Academic, 1981, p. 128.</ref>
The death of the sitting MP in 1919 led to a sensational by-election gain for the Labour Party, which was described by historian [[Maurice Cowling]] as the worst result for the Coalition during the 1918-22 Parliament;<ref>Maurice Cowling, "The Impact of Labour, 1920–1924", Cambridge University Press, 1971, p. 112.</ref> [[John Ramsden (historian)|John Ramsden]] admitted that Labour's win had a big psychological impact on the Coalition but thought the result was a "freak win" given that Labour had under 40% of the vote.<ref>John Ramsden, "Newport and the fall of the Coalition" in "By-Elections in British Politics", Macmillan Press, 1973, p. 18.</ref> At the ensuing general election, the ''[[Manchester Guardian]]'' described the constituency as "scattered between the three towns of Leeds, Bradford and Huddersfield", centred on Cleckheaton, and populated by "woollen and wire workers, miners, card manufacturers". A significant presence of Irish voters was also noted.<ref>"The Second Round in Spen Valley: Sir John Simon and Mr. Tom Myers", ''Manchester Guardian'', 9 November 1922, p. 12.</ref> Sir John Simon, a former Home Secretary who had lost his seat in the 1918 election, regained the seat for the Liberals in 1922 and held it until given a Peerage in 1940. During this period Simon moved from declaring his basic sympathy with the Labour Party's objects, to forming the [[National Liberal Party (UK, 1931)|Liberal National]]s who went into alliance with the Conservatives.<ref>David Dutton, "Liberals in Schism: A history of the National Liberal Party", Tauris Academic Studies, 2008, p. 42.</ref> Simon found his constituency marginal, and had a majority of under 1,000 in his last election, and Labour gained it in the 1945 election landslide.
Boundary changes abolished the constituency in 1950. The bulk of the abolished constituency, including Cleckheaton, Gildersome and Spenborough, formed the eastern half of [[Brighouse and Spenborough]]; another large part including Gildersome, Birstall and Drighlington, formed part of [[Batley and Morley]]. Heckmondwike and Mirfield transferred to [[Dewsbury (UK Parliament constituency)|Dewsbury]], while Kirkheaton moved to [[Colne Valley (UK Parliament constituency)|Colne Valley]] and other parts moved to [[Huddersfield East]].
==Boundaries== ===1885–1950=== While originally devised by the Boundary Commissioners in 1885, the division was originally named as 'Birstal', "from the name of a large ancient parish".<ref>"County of York (Eastern Division of the West Riding)" in "Report of the Boundary Commissioners for England Wales, 1885" (C.-4287), vol I p. 185-7.</ref> The naming of the new division led to a small struggle between the two Houses of Parliament during the passage of the [[Redistribution of Seats Act 1885]], when [[Alfred Illingworth]] (Liberal MP for [[Bradford (UK Parliament constituency)|Bradford]]) moved an amendment to replace 'Birstal' with 'Spen Valley'. Illingworth argued that Birstall contained only one-eighth of the population of the division, but Spen Valley was a name which represented several important towns, and his amendment was accepted without dissent by the House of Commons.<ref>''[https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1885/apr/16/england#S3V0296P0_18850416_HOC_234 Hansard]'' 3ser vol 296 col 1937.</ref> When the Bill reached the House of Lords, the Conservative peer the [[William Duncombe, 1st Earl of Feversham|Earl of Feversham]] moved an amendment to reinstate 'Birstal' claiming the support of the people in the area. The Earl contended that the Spen Valley was an unknown description and "was only remarkable for being the receptacle of all the sewage from Birstal", whereas Birstal was a very important parish. He had support from the [[Gathorne Gathorne-Hardy, 1st Earl of Cranbrook|Earl of Cranbrook]] and his amendment was also accepted without dissent.<ref>''[https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/lords/1885/jun/08/disqualification-of-voters-for-corrupt#S3V0298P0_18850608_HOL_142 Hansard]'' 3ser vol 298 col 1394.</ref>
When the Bill returned to the House of Commons, Alfred Illingworth again took up the issue and moved that the Commons disagree with the Lords. He again pointed to the small population of Birstall in comparison with other towns, and noted that the [[Sanitary district]] covering the area was known as Spen Valley and that the River Spen ran through the centre of the constituency whereas Birstall was in the extreme north-east corner of it. Conservative MP [[Edward Stanhope]] ([[Mid Lincolnshire]]) said that he had found feeling in the area to be in favour of 'Birstal', but the [[President of the Local Government Board]] [[Sir Charles Dilke]], speaking for the Government, stated that the local boards in Heckmondwike, Liversedge and Cleckheaton (where a majority of the population lived) had sent a memorial in favour of 'Spen Valley'. He agreed that the name had been invented by the Local Government Board, but argued that there were "local jealousies" between the towns and that Birstall was unpopular with the others, and therefore personally supported 'Spen Valley'. After a brief debate, the House voted by 65 to 46 to insist on 'Spen Valley' as the name.<ref>''[https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1885/jun/15/clause-a-acceleration-of-registration-in#S3V0298P0_18850615_HOC_188 Hansard]'', 3ser vol 298 cols 1581-2.</ref> The Lords then gave way, but not without further protest from the Earl of Feversham.<ref>''[https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/lords/1885/jun/23/consideration-of-commons-reasons#S3V0298P0_18850623_HOL_23 Hansard]'' 3ser vol 298 cols 1610-11.</ref>
During this battle no alteration was made to the boundary. The new division was to consist of: *the Parishes in the Sessional Division of [[Dewsbury]] of [[Gomersal]], [[Heckmondwike]] and [[Liversedge]], and *the Parishes of [[Cleckheaton]], [[Clifton, West Yorkshire|Clifton]], [[Hartshead]], and [[Wyke, Bradford|Wyke]].<ref>[[Redistribution of Seats Act 1885]]</ref>
When redefined by the Boundary Commission in 1917, the county division was defined as consisting of the [[Urban district (Great Britain and Ireland)|Urban District]]s of [[Birkenshaw, West Yorkshire|Birkenshaw]], [[Birstall, West Yorkshire|Birstall]], [[Drighlington]], [[Gildersome]], [[Heckmondwike]], Hunsworth, [[Kirkheaton]], [[Lepton, West Yorkshire|Lepton]], [[Mirfield]], [[Spenborough]] and Whitley Upper.<ref>"46. County of York, West Riding" in "Report of the Boundary Commission (England and Wales)", Cd. 8757, vol II.</ref>
The effect of the boundary change in 1918 was as shown in the table:
{|class="wikitable" |- style="background-color:#E9E9E9" | | '''Parish''' || '''1911 Population''' || '''1885–1918''' || '''1918–1950''' || '''Notes''' |- | Birkenshaw ||align=right| 2,508 || Spen Valley || Spen Valley || Was part of Gomersal Parish in 1885 |- | Birstall ||align=right| 7,116 || Spen Valley || Spen Valley || Was part of Gomersal Parish in 1885 |- | Cleckheaton ||align=right| 12,866 || Spen Valley || Spen Valley || Part of Spenborough Urban District from 1915 |- | Clifton ||align=right| 2,258 || Spen Valley || Elland || |- | Drighlington ||align=right| 4,126 || Pudsey || Spen Valley || |- | Gildersome ||align=right| 2,981 || Pudsey || Spen Valley || |- | Gomersal ||align=right| 3,796 || Spen Valley || Spen Valley || Included Birkenshaw and Birstall in 1885 |- | Hartshead ||align=right| 958 || Spen Valley || Elland || |- | Heckmondwike ||align=right| 9,016 || Spen Valley || Spen Valley || |- | Hipperholme (part) ||align=right| 322 || Spen Valley || Elland || Part of Wyke parish in 1885, removed in 1899 |- | Hunsworth ||align=right| 1,326 || Pudsey || Spen Valley || |- | Kirkheaton ||align=right| 2,621 || Holmfirth || Spen Valley || |- | Lepton ||align=right| 2,999 || Holmfirth || Spen Valley || |- | Liversedge ||align=right| 14,658 || Spen Valley || Spen Valley || Part of Spenborough Urban District from 1915 |- | Mirfield ||align=right| 11,712 || Morley || Spen Valley || |- | Whitley Upper ||align=right| 830 || Holmfirth || Spen Valley || |- | Wyke ||align=right| 6,145 || Spen Valley || Bradford South || |}
Of the 59,643 population in Spen Valley before the boundary change, 49,960 (83.8%) remained in the division after it. 6,145 (10.3%) moved to Bradford South while 3,538 (5.9%) moved to Elland. The new constituency was made up primarily of the old Spen Valley (65.3%), with 11,712 (15.3%) from Morley, 8,433 (11.0%) from Pudsey, and 6,450 (8.4%) from Holmfirth.
=== 2024–present === '''2024–present''': The Borough of Kirklees wards of: Birstall and Birkenshaw; Cleckheaton; Dalton (polling district DA06); Heckmondwike; Liversedge and Gomersal; Mirfield.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2023/1230/schedules/made |at=Schedule 1 Part 9 Yorkshire and the Humber region}}</ref>
[[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]] described changes to the constituency as following: ''The majority of the electorate will come from the current seat of [[Batley and Spen]] - excluding the town of [[Batley]] itself. To compensate for this loss, [[Mirfield]] will be transferred in from the [[Dewsbury (UK Parliament constituency)|Dewsbury]] constituency and the small part of Dalton ward, which includes the village of [[Kirkheaton]] will come from [[Huddersfield (UK Parliament constituency)|Huddersfield]].''

{{Short description|Parliamentary constituency in the United Kingdom}} {{Use dmy dates|date=July 2024}} {{Use British English|date=November 2019}} {{Infobox UK constituency main |name = Thirsk and Malton |parliament = uk |image = {{maplink|frame=yes|frame-align=center|plain=yes|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/Thirsk and Malton (UK Parliament constituency)}}|frame-height=200|frame-width=250}} |caption = Boundaries since 2024 |image2 = [[File:Yorkshire and the Humber - Thirsk and Malton constituency.svg|215px|alt=Map of constituency]] |caption2 = Boundary of Thirsk and Malton in Yorkshire and the Humber |year = 2010 |abolished = |elects_howmany = One |type = County |previous = [[Ryedale (UK Parliament constituency)|Ryedale]] (majority)
[[Vale of York (UK Parliament constituency)|Vale of York]] (part) |next = |year2 = 1885 |abolished2 = 1983 |elects_howmany2 = One |previous2 = [[Thirsk (UK Parliament constituency)|Thirsk]] and [[Malton (UK Parliament constituency)|Malton]]; preceded by [[North Riding of Yorkshire (UK Parliament constituency)|North Riding of Yorkshire]] |next2 = [[Ryedale (UK Parliament constituency)|Ryedale]], [[Richmond (Yorks) (UK Parliament constituency)|Richmond (Yorks)]], [[Selby (UK Parliament constituency)|Selby]] and [[Skipton and Ripon (UK Parliament constituency)|Skipton and Ripon]]{{cite web|title='Thirsk and Malton', Feb 1974 – May 1983|url=http://electionweb.co.uk/Bp/P74571.htm|website=ElectionWeb Project|publisher=Cognitive Computing Limited|accessdate=24 March 2016}} |electorate = 79,964 (December 2019){{cite web|url=https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/parliament-and-elections/elections-elections/uk-elections/constituency-data-electorates/|title=Constituency data: electorates – House of Commons Library|date=15 June 2020|publisher=Parliament UK|access-date=22 July 2020}} |region = England |county = [[North Yorkshire]] |towns = [[Pickering, North Yorkshire|Pickering]], [[Filey]], [[Thirsk]], [[Easingwold]], [[Malton, North Yorkshire|Malton]] |mp = [[Kevin Hollinrake]] |party = }} '''Thirsk and Malton''' is a [[Constituencies of the Parliament of the United Kingdom|constituency]] in [[North Yorkshire]] represented in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|UK Parliament]] since [[2015 United Kingdom general election|2015]] by [[Kevin Hollinrake]], a [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]]. ==History== ===2010–2015=== [[Anne McIntosh]], a Conservative, elected for Vale of York in 1997 then in Thirsk and Malton in 2010, having defeated fellow MP [[John Greenway (MP)|John Greenway]] in the selection, qualified as an advocate and worked for six years as political adviser to the [[European Democrats]] group in Brussels, then won election as an [[Member of the European Parliament|MEP]] for two terms. Since 2010, she chaired the [[Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Select Committee]]. In 2014, she was deselected as the Conservative candidate. In 2015, [[Kevin Hollinrake]] was elected as MP. ===Political history=== [[Image:ThirskAndMaltonConstituency1918.gif|thumb|250px|Thirsk and Malton in North Yorkshire 1918–50]] Traditionally a [[safe seat|safe Conservative seat]], the main forerunner, Ryedale (abolished in 2010) was taken by [[Elizabeth Shields]] for the [[Liberal Party (UK)|Liberal Party]], following a [[1986 Ryedale by-election|by-election in 1986]], held following the death of MP [[John Spence (politician)|John Spence]], and she held it for one year until the 1987 general election. [[Robin Turton, Baron Tranmire|Robin Turton]] was the [[Secretary of State for Health|Minister of Health]] (note head of department in that era) from December 1955 to January 1957. He also became [[father of the House]] and was among the longest-serving MPs for a single constituency, representing his seat for 44 years and 9 months. ==Boundaries== {{maplink|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/Thirsk and Malton (UK Parliament constituency) 2010}}|frame=yes|frame-height=250|text=Map of 2010–2024 boundaries}} '''1918–1950''': The Urban District of Malton, the Rural Districts of Easingwold, Flaxton, Helmsley, Kirkbymoorside, Malton, Thirsk, and Wath, and part of the Rural District of Pickering. '''1950–1974''': The Urban District of Malton, the Rural Districts of Bedale, Easingwold, Flaxton, Helmsley, Kirkbymoorside, Malton, Thirsk, and Wath, and part of the Rural District of Pickering. '''1974–1983''': The Urban District of Malton, and the Rural Districts of Bedale, Easingwold, Flaxton, Helmsley, Kirkbymoorside, Malton, Thirsk, and Wath. ''The constituency was abolished before [[1983 United Kingdom general election|1983 elections]]'' ''The constituency war re-established by [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]]'' '''2010–2024''': The District of Ryedale, the District of Hambleton wards of Easingwold, Helperby, Huby and Sutton, Shipton, Sowerby, Stillington, Thirsk, Thorntons, Tollerton, Topcliffe, White Horse, and Whitestonecliffe, and the Borough of Scarborough wards of Filey and Hertford. '''2024–present''': The District of Hambleton wards of: Bagby & Thorntons; Bedale; Sowerby & Topcliffe; Tanfield; Thirsk; the District of Ryedale: Amotherby; Ampleforth; Cropton; Dales; Derwent; Helmsley; Hovingham; Kirkbymoorside; Malton; Norton East; Norton West; Pickering East; Pickering West; Rillington; Ryedale South West; Sherburn; Sheriff Hutton; Sinnington; Thornton Dale Ryedale; and Wolds; and the Borough of Scarborough wards of: Filey; Hunmanby.{{cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2023/1230/schedules/made |at=Schedule 1 Part 9 Yorkshire and the Humber region}} [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]] the constituency described as following: ''In order to bring its electorate within the permitted range, the south-western part of the constituency, including [[Easingwold]], will be included in the newly created constituency of [[Wetherby and Easingwold (UK Parliament constituency)|Wetherby and Easingwold]]. To partly compensate, [[Bedale]] and [[West Tanfield|Tanfield]] will be added from [[Richmond (Yorks) (UK Parliament constituency)|Richmond (Yorks)]] – to be renamed [[Richmond and Northallerton (UK Parliament constituency)|Richmond and Northallerton]].'' ==Constituency profile== The seat also includes [[Pickering, North Yorkshire|Pickering]] and most of the [[North York Moors]] (its southern part), a mixed rugged crags and hillside [[National Park]]; its coastline in the seat at [[Filey]] is where the Moors meets the sea, with picturesque bays near to [[Scarborough, North Yorkshire|Scarborough]]. [[Electoral Calculus]] describes the seat as "Strong Right", characterised by support for socially conservative values and [[Brexit]].{{cite web|url=https://www.electoralcalculus.co.uk/fcgi-bin/seatdetails.py?seat=Thirsk+and+Malton|title=Thirsk and Malton: Seat Details|website=Electoral Calculus|accessdate=7 September 2022}} ==Members of
